title: Geometry of a monomial trait model with a generically invertible exponent
statement:
A trait is $S=\operatorname{Spec}R$ with $R$ a Noetherian local domain of dimension one and principal maximal ideal; a uniformizer $\pi$ generates that maximal ideal. Let $n\geq1$ and $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbf N$, with at least one $a_i$ nonzero and invertible in the fraction field $K$ of $R$. Put
$$B=R[T_1,\ldots,T_n]/(\prod_i T_i^{a_i}-\pi).$$
Then $B$ is a Noetherian integral domain and a regular ring [def-weil-regular-scheme, def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], and $\operatorname{Spec}B\to S$ has smooth generic fibre [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]. Zero exponents are allowed. Polynomial rings and spectra mean [def-weil-polynomial-ring, def-weil-affine-spectrum]. No excellence or henselianity assumption is made.

proof.text:
Write $P=R[T_1,\ldots,T_n]$, $M=\prod_iT_i^{a_i}$ and $f=M-\pi$, so $B=P/(f)$ as in [def-per-monomial-trait-model]. Since $R$ is Noetherian and $B$ is a finite-type $R$-algebra, [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra-noetherian] makes $B$ Noetherian. The local ring $R$ is regular directly from [def-weil-regular-scheme]: it has dimension one and maximal ideal $(\pi)$. Also $\pi
e0$ and $\pi
otin(\pi)^2$: an equation $\pi=\pi^2r$ in this domain would imply $1=\pi r$, contradicting that $\pi$ belongs to the maximal ideal. For later fibre identifications, [lem-weil-pbc-krull-intersection-jacobson], applied to the finite module $R$ over itself and its maximal ideal $(\pi)$, gives $ igcap_r\pi^rR=0$. Hence every nonzero $x\in R$ has a largest $v$ with $x\in\pi^vR$; writing $x=\pi^v u$ forces $u
otin(\pi)$, so $u$ is a unit. Thus $R[1/\pi]=K$.

source.place: Expose XVI Lemma 3.5.13(i), pp.250--251, exercise; setup; supporting Stacks Algebra Tag 00FN (lemma-Noetherian-permanence), and Definition 00KU.

proof.text: The generic fibre has coordinate ring $C=K\otimes_R B=K[T_1,\ldots,T_n]/(f)$: extension of coefficients and the quotient maps give mutually inverse maps on the displayed generators. Choose $j$ with $a_j>0$ and $a_j\in K^\times$. In $C$, $M=\pi\in K^\times$, so every $T_i$ with $a_i>0$ is a unit. Consequently $\partial f/\partial T_j=a_j\pi T_j^{-1}$ is a unit. Reorder $T_j$ first. This one-equation presentation is standard smooth by [def-weil-pbc-standard-smooth-algebra], hence $C$ is a smooth $K$-algebra by [lem-weil-pbc-standard-smooth-is-smooth]. Every prime localization of $C$ is regular local by [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-over-field-regular-local].

source.place: Expose XVI Lemma 3.5.13(i), pp.250--251, exercise; generic-fibre Jacobian; supporting Stacks Algebra Tags 00T6 (definition-standard-smooth), 00T7 (lemma-standard-smooth), 00TT (lemma-characterize-smooth-over-field).

proof.text: To check smoothness in the scheme convention, the finite displayed presentation gives local finite presentation by [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation]. For any $K$-algebra $D$ and ideal $J$ with $J^2=0$, lift the images of the $T_i$ of a map $C\to D/J$ to $t_i\in D$. Then $f(t)\in J$ and $d=(\partial f/\partial T_j)(t)$ is a unit: an inverse modulo $J$ lifts to an inverse since $1+z$ has inverse $1-z$ for $z\in J$. Replacing $t_j$ by $t_j-d^{-1}f(t)$ and fixing the other variables kills $f$ by polynomial expansion, because every quadratic term in the correction lies in $J^2=0$. This gives a lift $C\to D$. By [lem-weil-pbc-affine-formally-smooth-iff-ring-lifting], $\operatorname{Spec}C\to\operatorname{Spec}K$ is formally smooth, hence smooth by [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms].

source.place: Expose XVI Lemma 3.5.13(i), pp.250--251, exercise; explicit square-zero lifting for the generic fibre; supporting Stacks More on Morphisms Tag 02H4 (lemma-affine-formally-smooth) and Definition 02H0.

proof.text: Let $\mathfrak q\subset P$ be any prime containing $f$ and $\pi$. Since $M\in\mathfrak q$, choose $i$ with $a_i>0$ and $T_i\in\mathfrak q$. Put $Q=P_{\mathfrak q}$ with maximal ideal $\mathfrak n$. The contraction of $\mathfrak q$ to $R$ is $(\pi)$, so [lem-trf-polynomial-localization-order-reflection] makes $Q$ regular local. Quotienting by $T_i$ gives a polynomial ring $P'=R[T_h:h\ne i]$ and a prime $\mathfrak q'$ whose contraction is again $(\pi)$. The same order-reflection lemma, now on $P'_{\mathfrak q'}$, shows that $\pi$ is not in its squared maximal ideal. The natural map $Q\to P'_{\mathfrak q'}$ sends $f$ to $-\pi$ and sends $\mathfrak n^2$ into that squared ideal. Therefore $f\notin\mathfrak n^2$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-regular-local-hypersurface-criterion] and [lem-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime-of-quotient] to obtain that the corresponding local ring of $B$ is regular. Every other prime of $B$ avoids $\pi$ and has local ring equal to a prime localization of $C$ (invert $\pi$ and then the remaining denominators); these are regular by step 2. Thus $B$ is regular. This also covers $n=1$, when $P'=R$.

source.place: Expose XVI Lemma 3.5.13(i), pp.250--251, exercise; special-fibre local calculation; supporting Stacks Algebra Tags 031E and 00NO as in the order-reflection lemma; Tag 00NQ (lemma-regular-ring-CM), Tag 00CT (proposition-localize-quotient).

proof.text: Apply [lem-per-monomial-quotient-normal-basis] to $(A,c,a)=(R,\pi,a)$. Thus $B$ has the $R$-basis of monomials $T^b$ with $b\not\geq a$ componentwise. In these coordinates $\pi^rB$ consists exactly of finite coefficient families in $\pi^rR$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-krull-intersection-jacobson] to the finite $R$-module $R$ and its maximal ideal $(\pi)$ to get $\bigcap_r\pi^rR=0$. Taking coefficients yields $\bigcap_r\pi^rB=0$. This argument uses finite generation only for $R$ over itself, not for the generally infinite-rank $R$-module $B$.

source.place: Expose XVI Lemma 3.5.13(i), pp.250--251, exercise; connectedness input; monomial coordinates and Stacks Algebra Tag 00IQ (lemma-intersection-powers-ideal-module), part (2).

proof.text: Put $k=R/(\pi)$. Reduction of coefficients identifies $B/\pi B$ with $k[T_1,\ldots,T_n]/(M)$; the normal basis of step 5 gives this identification coefficient by coefficient. The quotient is graded by total degree because $(M)$ is homogeneous of positive degree, and its degree-zero part is $k$. If $u^2=u$ in this quotient, its constant term is $0$ or $1$. After replacing $u$ by $1-u$ assume it is $0$. If $u\ne0$, let $d>0$ be its least nonzero homogeneous degree. The degree-$d$ part of $u^2$ is zero, contradicting $u^2=u$. Hence the only idempotents in $B/\pi B$ are $0,1$. For an idempotent $e\in B$, replace $e$ by $1-e$ if necessary so $e\in\pi B$. Since $e=e^r\in\pi^rB$ for every $r\ge1$, step 5 implies $e=0$. Thus $B$ has no idempotents other than $0,1$.

source.place: Expose XVI Lemma 3.5.13(i), pp.250--251, exercise; elementary graded calculation and idempotent separation, supplied to complete the exercise; no completeness or henselianity is used.

proof.text: The assignment $R\to k$ and $T_i\mapsto0$ kills $f$ because $a\ne0$, giving a surjection $B\to k$. Its kernel is prime, so $X=\operatorname{Spec}B$ is nonempty. By [def-weil-affine-spectrum], $\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)=B$. Step 6 and [lem-pc-scheme-connected-iff-idempotents] show $X$ connected. It is regular by step 4 and [def-weil-regular-scheme]. Apply [lem-sc-regular-connected-integral] to obtain that $X$ is integral. Finally [def-pc-integral-scheme], applied to the nonempty affine open $X$ itself, says that $B$ is an integral domain. Together with steps 1--4 this proves all assertions.

source.place: Expose XVI Lemma 3.5.13(i), pp.250--251, exercise; integrality from connectedness and regularity; supporting Stacks Properties Tags 0569 (lemma-regular-normal), 033N (lemma-normal-locally-Noetherian), 01OK (definition-integral).
